SPAIN The English Minister at Madrid has notified to the Spanish Minister of Foreign Affairs that the British Consul at the Canaries has received instructions to pay to the captain of the Spanish vessel Adan .£20 for the maintenance of the I crew of the English schooner Betsey, who, when this vessel went on shore on the coast of Africa, werA taken on board the former vessel. £100 will also be distributed as a compensation amongst the crew of the Adan. The conduct of the Spanish sailors in this affair was mosi commendable Engaged in fishing on the const, they were made aware of the English schooner being on shore, and that the captain had been seized by the natives. Armed only with the instruments of their calling, they landed on the coast, penetrated into the inj terior, and released the English captain, whom | they discoveted bound and buried in the earth up to the waist. Tl ey delivered him again to 1 his crew, assisted in getting off the, schooner, , and retired without accepting any recompense whatever.

I glanced upward to his face : his eye was fixed, and looked steadfastly in one direction þÿ as though it would pierce the sheet of flame, that rolled further and further from where we

stood, and nearer to the fatal spot. The expres sion of that eyo was fearful to behold ; it was a of concentrated agony. A single tear had escaped Irom it, and was rolling down the rude weather-bronzed oheek, little used to such bedewing. The broad chest was heaving in short quick spasms, and it was evident the roan was struggling with his breath. He was listening through all this intensity of þÿgaze listening for the death-shriek of his old comrade þÿ his bosomfriend ! Not long was the suspense ; though there was no shriek, no cry of human voice, to indicate the face of the fire, and, unless he had started long j crisis. If any arose, it was not heard by us. only to look for his bones amoug the smouldering ashes. Up to this moment, Garey had stood in a fixed attitude, silent aDd rigid as a statue. perils þÿ like thoughts and habitudes þÿ though pergood deal unlike all had combined to unite the haps dispositions, þÿ age, and characters were a two in a firm bond of friendship. This Estate has been established but very recently, and is situated in one of the most fertile parts of the Island of Vieques ; it is about a quarter of au hour's journey distant from the town, and has a good road which communicates with Porto Negro, its port for shipment. It contains about 1,200 cuerdas, whereof 200 are planted in Canes, 100 in pasturage, and the remainder in Virgin Forest containing the choicest kinds of wood tor building purposes. In addition to some slaves, the Estato has an establishment ot about 60 free labourers who are bound by contract for one and two years, subject to a renewal ; the great advantages of comfort and an abundant supply of water renders it peculiarly favorable to the wants ot the free labourers of the place in addition to

being well found in all two there are respects as a com- fine Mills, one plete Estate, steam worked by of 12 horse power, the other a Cattle Mill ; the works are supplied with Clarifiers and a spare Boiler, so that in case of accident there can be no suspension of work. The pasturage supports 50 yoke of working Cattle, and in addition to the natural Springs, there is a Cistern ot about 900 puncheons. Twenty-three new wooden Houses for labourers, residences for Masters and Overseers, Boiling and Curing House, Carts ; all necessary implements as per Inventory will be delivered in good order. CHAPTER XXIX. THE MESA. After a breakfast of buffalo-flesh, seasoned with splendid appetites, and t. hed down by a cup of cold water from the arr we þÿ saddled þÿup, and headed for a high b tc, just visible over the plain. My companion ..new the landmark well. It lay directly in our route. We should pass near its base and a ride of ten miles further would bring us to th . d ol our journey ; indeed, the einineneo was wi in sight ot the raneheria. From the roof ui þÿalcalde house. s I had frequently noticed it in clear weather only was it visible, outlined ugain.it the horizon, in a north-westerly direction from the village Struck with the singularity of this prairiemound, I had projected a visit to it ; hut circum stances had prevented me from carrying out my intention I was now to have the pleasure of a nearer acquaintance with it. I have called it singular. Most isolated hills arc conical, dome-shaped, or ridge like ; this one differed from the usual configuration þÿ hence its singularity. It presented tlie appearance of a huge box set upon the prairie, not unlike that rare formation, the þÿ cofre, which crowns the summit of the mountain Pcrote. Its sides in the distance appeared perfectly vertical, and its top horizontal as the plain on which it rested As we drew nearer, I could perceive by the dark parapet-like hand along its crest that it was

covered with a growth of timber. T his was the more readily observed from contrast with the perpendicular sides, which were almost of a snowy whiteness, on account of the gypsum, chalk, r milky quartz of which the rock was composed The most peculiar feature of the mound was per haps its apparently regular form þÿ a perfect, parallelopipedon Rut it was striking in other respect" Its sides glistened fantastically under the rays of the sun, as though it werestudde l with windows ot glass. This, however, was easily accounted for; and I knew that the sparkling effect was produced by plates of mica or sclen> » that entered into the composition of the rock 1 had seen whole mountains that presented similar appearance. More than one such exi, u in the great American Suara, in whose glittering cliffs, viewed from afar, may be found the origin of that wild chimera, the mountain of gold Although neither a mountain of gold norsilvthe mound in question was an object of ram ioterest. A very enchanted castle did it appeal, and it was difficult to assign its formation t nature alone. Unman agency, one could u. . help fancying, must have hud something to do u piling up a structure so regular and compact But lie who has travelled over much of th þÿearth surface s will have met with many þÿ freaks of nature, exhibiting like appearance of design, in her world of inorganic matter. It was in fact, one of those formations of which many arc met with in the plateaux-lands of America, known in Spanish phraseology as mesas. This name is

given to them in allusion to the flat table-lik> tops, which distinguish them from other ch v.it d summits. Sometimes one of these mesas is found hundreds of miles from any similar emiutucc more frequently a number of them stand near each other, like truncated þÿcones the summits of all being on the same level, and often covered with a vegetation differing materially from that of the surrounding plains. Geologists have al firmed that these table-tops are the ancient leve of the plains themselves ; and that all around, and intervening between them, lias cither sunk or submitted to the degradation ot water! It i< a vague explanation, and scarcely satisfies I hr speculative mind. The mesa of Mexico is still a geological puzzle. As wc approached ibis singular object. I coni 1 not help regarding it witli a degree of curiosity 1 had seen mesa heights before þÿ in the þÿ muuvnise þÿterre, upon the Missouri, in the Navajo country west of the Rocky Mountains, and along the edges of the þÿ Llano þÿEstacado, which of itself is a vast mesa. The mound before ii" was peculiar, from its very regular form, and the sparkling sheen of its cliffs. Its complete isolation, more over, added to the effect for no other cniineuc þÿ appeared in sight. The low hills that bordered the Rio Grande could barely lie distinguished m the distance.

On getting nearer to if, its character became somewhat altered; the square hux-like form ap peared less regular, and it was then perceived that the parallelopipedon was not perfect. Slight ledges could be traced traversing the face i fit" cliffs, ami here and there the retangular linos were broken to the rye. Nature, after all, had not been so exact in her architecture. Yet, with every deduction, it was a singular structure to look upon, not the less so that its summit was inaccessible to human foot. \ precipice fifty yards sheer fronted outward on all sides ; no one had ever scaled this precipice þÿ so alleged my companions, who were well acquainted with the locality We had approached within less than a mile of its base; our conversation had dropped þÿ ar least so f ir as I was concerned; my thoughts wenoccupied with the mound, and my eyes wandered over its outlines. I was endeavouring to make out the character of the vegetation which sepuie i to flourish luxuriantly on its summit. The dark foliage was evidently that of some species of acicular trees, perhaps the common red cedar Ju niperus Virginiana) ; but there were others o| lighter hue -in all likelihood pmons, the pirn s with edible cones, peculiar to this region. I noticed, also, growing upon the very edge of tin S cliff, yuccas and aloes, whose radiating blades, stretching out, curved gracefully over the white rock. Forms of cactus, too, were apparent, and several plants of the great pitahaya rose high above the cliff, like gigantic candelabra, strange

Gradually, and without aiiy apparent cause, the Churches, throughout a vast extent of territory, were filled with worshipers. Absorbed in my supreme happiness, I took no heed of aught else ; I noticed neither track nor

path. Had I left tny horse to himself, most likely be would have taken the right road ; but in my reverie, perhaps I had mechanically dragged upon tho rein, and turned him from it. Whether or not, after a lapse of time, I found myself in the midst of thick woods, with not the semblance of a trail to guide me; and 1 knew not whether 1 was riding in the right direction. I ought rather to say that T kuew the contrary þÿ else 1 should long sineo have reached the clearings around the village. YVithout much reflection, 1 turned in a new direction, and rode for some time without striking a trail. This led me once more into doubt, and I made head back again, but still without success. 1 was in a forest-plain, but I could find no path leading anywhere; and amid the underwood of palmettoes I could not see any great distance arouud me. Beyond a question, 1 had strayed far out of my w ij. At an early hour of the day, this would have given me little concern ; but the sun had now set, and already, under the shadow of the mosscovcred trees, it was nearly dark Night would be down in a few minutes, and in all probability 1 should be obliged to spend it in the forest þÿ bv no means an agreeable prospect, and the less so that I was thinly clad and hungry. True, I the pleasant incident of the day 1 might dreari might pass some hours in sweet þÿ reflection upon rosy dreams þÿ -but, alas ! the soul is sadly undei the influence of the body ; tho spiritual must ever yield to the physical, and even love itself

becomes a victim to the vulgar appetite of hunger. I began to fear that, after all, I should have but a sorry night of it. I should be too hungry to think ; too cold either to sleep or dream ; besides, I was likely to get wet to the shirt : the rain had commenced failing in large heavy drops. After another unsuccessful effort to strike a trail, I pulled up and sat listening. My eyes would no longer avail me ; perhaps my ears might do better service. And so it chanced. The report of a rifle reached them, apparently fired some hundred yards off in the woods. Considering that l was upon hostile ground, ruoIi a sound might have caused me alarm ; but I knew from the sharp whip-like crack that the piece was a þÿhunter rifle, s and no Mexican ever handled a gun of that kind. Moreover, I had heard, closely following upon the shot, a dull concussion, as of some haavy body dropped from a high elevation to the ground. I was hunter enough to know the signification of this sound t was the game þÿ bird or beast þÿ that had fallen to the bullet. To bo continued

We have not hitherto been very sanguine as to the result of diplomacy with the Chinese Empire, but at least our negotiators have now made a step in advance They have so far

IN o i o i I trampled Chinese etiquette under foot ns to communicate directly with the higher authorities. The four Commissioners have succeeded j in delivering their credentials to tho provincial Governor of Soutchou-fou, who is in direct and easy relations with the Imperial Court at Pekin, The result is that the real state of the case is brought under the notice of b Emperor, who, but for this bold step, might for years to come have remained in ignorance of the real nature of the late operations at Canton The Emperor lias at once superseded, or rather degraded, 1 vernor Yeh, and has appointed General of Kwangtung and þÿKwangsi þÿ in his place as Goa certain Hwang Tsunghai, who s favourably known as a person of superior enlightenment and liberality of opinion, 'i his prow s that the Emperor amt his immediate advisers are beginning to appreciate the momentous character of the questions which they are now called upon to discuss with the outer world. They will appoint, as it is said, without delay, a Commissioner on their part to negotiate with the Commissioners of the Four Powers at Shanghai. We can scarcely anticipate that the Chinese Commissioner will be prepared to accede to the demands which will he made upon his Govern- 1 but for this we must be prepared. All the usual machinery of trickery, evasion, and dilatoriness will surely be tried again ; it rests only with the four Commissioners to frustrate these designs, and to insist upon an immediate solution of the questions at issue We must

not permit ourselves for one moment to be the dupes of the idle forms and ceremonies in which til,- Chinese delight, but go at once to the mark, whatever it may be. No answer or a delayed answer is a refusal. It operates as such, and as such it should he understood Firmness and decision in negotiation, backed by immediate action, when necessary, constitute on our side the only elements of success in our negotiations with these semi barbarians, who seem in their own persons to unite the rude cunning , deer-meat, of the savage with the polished craft of the < civilized man. We shall be much surprised if it does not eventually the Chinese as we require is a matter far less | venison þÿ

150 years, one might presume it to be. Mr. Oliphant and M. de þÿC ontades, who conveyed the notes of the Four Powers to Soutchou-fou, j to the although unguarded, experienced no incivility or violence from the Chinese in the course of their passage to and IVo. They passed along canals for two days, and at la-t reached the great city of Sou-tchou-fou, which they describe as being about the size of London. The Goþÿvernor palace s stands in the centre of the city, and to this spot they were conducted along streets crowded with spectators for a length ot two miles. Much interest, and something of wonder, might be discerned on the fares of this mighty crowd, but there was perfect silence and orderly behaviour The Governor received the emissaries with salutes, placed ! them in seats of honour, and feasted them with Chinese delicacies The next day he returned their visit, when they plied him witli cham pagne and other good things. In due course they took their leave, and departed on their return to Shanghai, having been completely successful as to the object of their mission If

these preliminary measures be carried out in more essential matters, we should have good hopes of a speedy and satisfactory result The Chinese people themselves are probably we.llto enter into commercial rela tions with us. THE FRENCH GOVERNMENT. (From the Times. It can serve no good purpose for us to avoid allusion to a matter which has become the subject of common conversation, and which may at any time produce consequences important to ourselves. The position of the French government and the state of things which now exists in Paris aro notoriously the cause of much uneasiness throughout Europe. The feeling must 111 turally be strongest in this country. We are close neighbours of France ; we are joined to the French people politically and commercially ; we are not only their allies, acting with them on several great European questions, but, which is of even more importance, the two communities are united by commercial relations, which affect the int rests directly or indirectly of half the families in England. The prices of French funds and French railway shares are quoted every day on the London market, our manufactures supply the French with a number of articles, and our people take other articles in return. Then, the E iglisli are f>,nd of travelling and excursions ; Paris is within 12 hours of London, and they have of late years come to consider a visit to the French capital as a pleasant way of spendiuga few days which they may have to spare. So, while fully admiring that no nation has aright to interfere in ;h- domestic concerns of France, we must he allowed to express our sorrow at the system of government which is being organised in that country, and to raise a voice of remonstrance, while there is yet time. This we. do

with r.o feeling of hostility to the existing authorities, but in, rely in the interest of quiet and good order in Europe. Common sense, when not blinded by fear of the intoxication of power, must point out how dangerous are elaborate schemos of gurveilance and repression, and how hopeless is the attempt to check the tongues or watch the movements cf many millions of people. We are told that the Ministry of Police is to be reorganised, and that its chief will be placed in the lirst rank of ministers. He should, indeed, take precedence of them all, everything seems likely to be brought within the sphere of his control. The gay city of Paris, the homo of social intercourse, of lively conversation and free opinions, hardly knows itself. The outward aspect of the place is the same ; there are the same Boulevards, the same fountains hashing in the sun, the same cafes frequented by the same i loungers, and in private life the same drawingrooms, and hangings, and toilets. But over everything there are gloom and uneasiness People are talking timidly and with unusual dullness unusually common-place topics Families are hesitating whom they shall visit and whom they shall be visited by. Men consider i whether they ought to be seen walking with a friend whom they have known for years. Two persons will be speaking together, and on seeing a third about to join them will suddenly pause and turn the conversation There will be in the midst of a social concourse a man who checks the mirth and puts a guard on every tongue. People

will talk with him, shake hands with him, but they will be careful of what they say before hira. Individuals are careful what books they have in their libraries, what papers they have in their writing desks. They do not talk affably with their inferiors, as light hearted Frenchmen in the old times did. Tho concierge the waiter at the cafe, even the distance In a railway carriage it is as kept private servants, are well not at a to be too communicative with a neighbour. In a etter it is as well to confine yourself to your own

T-. & ft 0 I, A A. V ( private business and good wishes for your correspondent's health. For Paris and France aie under stiict surveilance, and no one knows who are the watchers and who are the watched. The Empire is espionnage Its incarnation is a mouchard. It is not only that recognised agents of police are in every street and every public place, that the comings and goings of well-known democrats are watched, that the assemblies of communists are hunted out, but men of every rank, every phase of character, every shade of political opinions, are at the mercy of an immense array of spies, who penetrate everywhere, who follow the individual into the confidence even of his family and his private life, and who have spread distrust and apprehension throughout the country. It has, indeed, long been the misfortune of France that the security of private relations has been weakened by the means used by government to obtain intelligence, and this fact has doubtless bad no little effect on society and domestic life; but it would seem that now tho evil has assumed fearful proportions. We hear of professional spies of every apparent rank in life, from the well dressed gentleuiau to the workman in his blouse ; we hear of loretles paid for information concerning those with whom they associate ; we bear of hotels and restaurants being frequented by persons whose duty it is to listen to the conversation of suspicious visitors, and to endeavour to draw them into an expression of

encouragement of domestic treachery by the corruption of private servants. From the, London Times, Friday , May 28 The French Emperor is likely to pay a high price, for military fidelity. The French people have not obtained without a sacrifice the order and tranquillity of which Imperialism boasts. Napoleon III. has delivered his country from the Parliamentary system ; he has expelled the virus of liberal institutions, suppressed the orgies of democracy, restrained the turbulence of petty ambitions, and so on. He has established a throne, guarded by half a million of bayonets, which we are told can be directed by a gesture from him against either foreign enemies or the subverters of order at home. But the army, which has been the instrument of these great changes and is the basis of this overwhelming power, is learning its own streugth, and seems fully incliued to use it. We should not return to the subject of the late, duel were it a mere isolated act, or were it likely that a fitting punishment would fall on the chief wrongdoer. But we only express that public opinion which trembles and shrinks from an utterance in Paris when wo say that the circumstances of this unhappy affair, the animosity indicated by the numerous challenges, the steady purpose of Hyenne, and, more than all, the applause with which the deed ban been received throughout the French army, are signs of an evil day which is at hand for French society, and for all that is independent and in-

tellectual in the country. The slaughter of a young writer by a professional swordsman for a harmless joke is in itself a cruel and cowardly act; but we wish we could think that there was nothing deeper in the affair than the vengeance of a set of underbred men for a rather petulant satire. People in Paris feel, and no doubt correctly, that the outrage is but an indication of the passions which arc bubbling up in a vast, triumphant, ambition and idle army þÿ an army sundered io interest and feeling from the rest of the nation, which knows little of society beyond its barracks, eaves for no authority but that of the chief it b e- used to the throne, and is animated with a growing jealousy and contempt of the non-military classes which formerly wielded political power. The conduct of M. Hyenne has received the approval of the army in general. So strongly lias this feeling been shown that probably no attempt will be made to visit the action with punishment, or even to mark it with disgrace, it is possible that M Hyenne niav retire from the service, or the Moviteur say a few words against the practice of duelling, but that will be all. In short, the army have triumphed, and every one knows it, nor can we believe that the Miuisterial authorities are sorry that it should be so Henceforth there will be another check on the press, which may save the necessity of warnings, and deliver the Government from any unpopularity which frequent interferences might bring upon it. The army

as a body is the support of the Empire, and it would be a brilliant idea to make its officers, as individuals, a terror to opposition journalists, who may be called to account for a . chance expression, and fought by a regiment volunteering for the purpose. The army seems quite disposed to enter into such an arrangement, and an event which lias happened witliin the last few days is a proof of their good will in the cause. Gumming peaceably entered St. Lake City on the 1st ult , and that a considerable portion of the Mormons had already left, or were leaving, for some point in the South- West. THE AMERICAN FLAG. While our maritime rights must be maintained to their fullest extent, a pretended regard for those rights will not, we hope, be made a cover for the Slave-Trade That the

American flag is constantly abused for this purpose; that the slavers fitted out in the ports of Cuba are mostly if not entirely Ainerican-built ; and that they attempt to skulk to sea still in the character of American vessels, hoping in that way to escape risk and capture by the British cruisers þÿ these facts are perfectly notorious to everybody. If the doctrine set up by Mr. Cass, in his late letter to Lord Napier, that our vessels cannot be entered without the consent of the p rsons in charge from the cruisers of any foreign power þÿ not even for the purpose <>f ascertaining whether is to be adhered to, it would seetn to be so much the more incumbent upon us to do ourselves what the right of others to do þÿ to take care the American flag and the outward apof being an American vessel are not employed to facilitate a business which is not oily a violation of the treaty between Great Britain and Spain, hut which is also a breach

We should ourselves much prefer, For a variety of reasons, that the enforcement of our laws against he Slave-Trade should not be left, so far as the police of the . eas is concerned, clusively to Britisli cruisers. We quite gree with Secretary Cass, that such a state of tliii s cannot be submitted to by any independent nation without injury and dishonor; though it certainly appears to us that in this particular the injury and dishonor consist rather in our leaving our laws against the Slave-Trade to he enforced by others than in the fact that Undoubtedly, there aro many points as to which the interference of British naval officers to enforce our laws would he highly impertinent. Such would be the case with all laws þÿ as our revenue laws, for instance þÿ enacted exclusively for our own benefit and convenience. But these laws against the Slave-Trade do not seem to be of that sort. Great Britain and the United States | arc mutually bound by treaty to exert their best efforts for the suppression of this traffic; and Great Britain has, therefore, by virtue of this express stipulation, not to mention the general sentiment on this subject of the civilized world, an interest in the enforcement of our Suppose that piracy þÿ and by our law the Slave-Trade is piracy þÿ was as extensively carried on under the American flag, and in American-built vessels, as the Slave-Trade is, and with as little success in suppressing it on the part of our Government as is attained in the matter of the Slave-Trade, we should

hardly be surprised, perhaps we should hardly have a right to complain, that vessels under the American fiag suspected of piracy were occasionally overhauled by foreign cruisers, aud, suspicious circumstances appearing, were sent in for trial. The true way in such eases would seem to he to remove all occasion or pretense for foreign interference, by ourselves taking the matter in hand. Let us first make ourselves a vigorous and sincere attempt at the enforcement of our laws against the Slave- Trade before positively setting down our foot that Great Britain shall not he allowed to interfere in the matter.

THE WAR-TRAIL: a romance. BV CAPTAIN MAYNE REID. chapter lviii. 111e voyagkl'r. We were not long iu suspense. Again the f umuli rolled foresight of the old trapper proved unerring, up the sky one after another, until their black masses shrouded the moon. CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 2nd JULY, 1858. By the arrival at St. Thomas of the American barque lira, we have been furnished with intelligence from New York to the 5th June.

A serious difficulty prevailed at New Or- I leans, the particulars of which, as relates to the causes, are however not given. A Vigilance Committee had, by the latest intelligence, been chosen and the Municip al authority had been resigned by the Mayor. A large number of persons were marked by the Vigilance Committee for punishment, and fifty of these, with two cannon had taken possession of Canal Street. The demonstration is supposed to be mainly political in its character. The community, it ment. appears, lost all confidence in the City Govern- þÿ þÿCrime as the New Y'ork Times | affirms þÿ lias been unusually prevalent, and the have been unusually lax and inefficient in the administration þÿofjustice. It is even confidently affirmed that very many id' the public officers were men whose sympathies and actions were almost openly on the side of the organized gangs of ruffians, who have kept the city in turmoil, and rendered life and property utterly unsafe by their deeds I of violence and of blood.

(from out OWN CORRESPONDENT.) PLYMOUTH, May, 27. All t he preparations for the trial trip which is to precede by a few days the actual attempt lo submerge this cable are being rapidly completed here, and most probably ere these details are laid before the, public the whole squadron will have started It for their preliminary cruise in deep water was originally intended and expected that the vessels would leave the Sound on Thursday morning last, but one cause or another has occurred to frustrate tliis arrangement, and it is not now expected that tlie squadron will he clear off until to-morrow (Saturday) evening. The Agamemnon, Captain Precdy, and (lie Niagara, Captain Hudson, are lying within a few yards of eaeli other in Hnmonze, and the. Oorgon, Commander Dayman, and the Valorous, Captain Aldham, which have been appointed by the Admiralty to accompany and assist the expedition, are also anchored near at hand þÿ first two named are, of course, the vessels the The ones on board which the coil is stowed, and from which, in a few more days, it will either he laid or lost, as Providence may decide. Botli are now nearly ready for the voyage, and in both the peaceful nature of the expedition seems, judging from appearances, to sit with the most remarkably ill grace. Their heretofore spotless decks are all begrimed with tar and grease, and uncouth machinery and misshapen coils obstruct and lumber up the a places where a short time ago it was almost

breach of the articles of war to leave an untidylooking þÿrope s end or drop a spot of dirt. Even the hallowed precincts of the quarter decks themselves are become as places of no account, mere platforms for the erection of sheaved wheels to guide the tarry wire into its ocean bed. Nor are the changes which have taken place in the internal arrangements of I mental cruise to test its character and capabilieach ship of less importance. Wardrooms and gunrooms are almost words of no meaning ; cabins arc transferred and transformed, one ordinary room being knocked into a dozen for the accommodation of the officers, and a dozen rooms knocked into one for the accommodation of the cable. The latter trifle seems to occupy both ships in every part þÿ on the spar deck or on the keel, in cabins and almost in berths its monstrous tarry folds are always present, lying, coil above coil, for hundreds and hundreds of miles, till the eye is pained and the head made giddy in vain attempts to follow its endless circles. As may readily he imagined, with at least 2,500 tons dead weight on hoard each vessel, both the Agamemnon and Niagara are astonishingly deep. The lower deck ports of the former are very near the water, and they are all being fastened and caulked before starting. Hut iu spite of this the Agamemnon carries her slune infinitely better than her long black-looking rival of tin; United States, which is immersed very deeply indeed by her load. The Agamemnon now only draws 20 feet, or

actually one foot less than her draught at starting last year; hut even at this depth she bears herself well, and looks a noble ship, and one that should he seaworthy iu any weather. The Niagara, however, draws no less than 27 feet 2 inches aft, and this great draught effects a marvellous and most unpleasant change in her appearance, since it leaves her spar deck scared v s feet above the water's edge. In fact, tiic main deck is actually below the waþÿter s level, and if her lofty bulwarks, some nine or ten feet high, were, taken away, she would appear to be almost the very last vessel iu the world in which it was desirable to venture across tlie great Atlantic. So much lias been said about this Niagara, and such exaggela'ed rumours have been afloat respecting her , at once to this port, and when the ships fill up general capacity as a war steamer, that many nf our readers may he surprised to learn that a- a war steamer she is almost a total failure. There have been had bargains out of our own dockyards. Her share of the cable is admiral'll well distributed throughout her entire length, and thus, of course, any chance of

( >n that ship the great bulk of her share of the wire is stowed, as before, in her capacious hold. Last year it was all coiled in one immense circular mass, nearly 1 00 feet iu circumference. By this arrangement, however, the pressure of some 1,300 tons upon such a small surface was found to be greater than the ship would hear with safety, and it also conduced to her rolling to an extent that was dangerous to the process of submerging. To avoid this, therefore, the hold lias been enlarged, and the coil is now laid in a mass, about 60 feet long by some 45 feet wide and 20 feet deep, and every precaution lias been taken to prevent its fouling or coining up iu þÿ kinks" while paying out In addition to this coil there is vet to he one on the orlop de.ck of 95 miles, and there is one near the forecastle 230, and of a small one of 20 miles for the experimental cruise. The programme of the intended proceedings of the expedition may be very briefly told. According to present arrangements the vessels leave the Sound to-morrow evening, and get j with all speed into deep water. Directly they at e out of þÿ þÿsoundings (meaning in about 2,000 fathoms) a piece of waste cable will he passed from the Agamemnon to the Niagara, and a splice made. Only this experiment can teach practically the best method of effecting j and ice. For the important junction when in the middle of the Atlantic The cable will then he sunk from both vessels, and, after a variety of experiments have been made as to its strength, by means of running out, itc., the þÿ reeling þÿin machines will he set to work to attempt to coil it up again. This latter portiou of the task, j though not altogether impossible, is so full of difficulty that but little hopes are entertained of recovering the piece with which the experiments are made, and which, to the length of some 30 or 40 miles, will, there is little doubt, remain as a permanent ornament to the bottom of the Atlantic. The loss of the piece, however, is of no consequence, since, apart from the practical value of the results it will furnish, it can have no other use. It is a portion of

the coil lost in the attempt «f last year, am! which was so injured in hauling up from 1,000 fathoms as to become, electrically speaking, of no further value. This experimental trip (which is likely to last about six days) finished, the vessels return

with coal and water the Agamemnon will re 1 the honour and ceive her last coil of 95 miles ( making up the total quantity on hoard of both, exclusive of the shore ends, to 2,066V and, the final preparations being completed , the squadron will sail for the great undertaking about the 5th of June. Our readers nre of course aware that the cable will be submerged by botli ships from the centre of the Atlantic, instead of commencing from the Irish coast as was the ease last year. There are many strong reasons in favour of the present plan, which is the original one, and which, though abandoned for a time, was warinlv advocated last year by Mr. Bright, the engineer of the company. 'Flic chief advantage, of course, is that by laying from the centre by botli ships the whole operation can he finished in half the time, and therefore at half the risk from had weather which it would otherwise incur. The plan, however, is not without serious risks of its own, but the manner in which these are to bo met has not as yet been finally decided upon. The Niagara will he given an advantage over the Agamemnon of some 60 or 100 miles ; that is, the junction of the wires will not he made exactly midway between Valetitia and Newfoundland, hut at the distance we have mentioned nearer to the American shore. No attempt will he made to effect the splice until the weather is fair and the barometer rising. Once, however, that the centre piece is resting on the bottom, both vessels part and make all safe speed to

their respective shores. The rate at which the cable will be lowered out will not be allowed much to exceed five knots per hour. During the whole process, of course, signals to ascertain the perfect continuity of the coil will be passed from ship to ship, and all questions and answers regarding the rate of speed and state of weather with which each vessel meets kept regularly recorded. As regards the chances of had weather, the most careful and elaborate investigations have been made on this subject navy, by Lieutenant Maury, of the human and therefore, as far as United þÿStates foresight and science can go, the risks have been at least foreseen, and therefore partly guarded against. According to this officer and to the statistical tables of the Washington Observatory, where the whole subject of the frequency of gales,

fogs, ice, and lightning in each month for the whole North and South Atlantic has been com piled from upwards of 260,000 days of observations, it seems that in the mouths of January and February that part of the Atlantic that lies between England and the United States is the stormiest known sea in the world, and that along the telegraphic route there always occur at least five, and perhaps 10 gales of wind during the January of every year. In the summer season the part of the Atlantic to he traversed by the paying out steamer going west is almost entirely exempt from gales. On the contrary, along the eastern (European) half of the route there occur annually on the average at least two or three gales in the months of June or July. There is, however, scarcely any chance of gales in the month of August, except in approaching the Irish coast, when the chances of encountering one are about as 3 to 30. On the other hand, the. steamer going west with the cable, though much less likely to encounter a gale, ha» to contend with almost as great dangers from fogs ice, it appears from the logbooks for some 830 summer voyages between Valentin and Newfoundland that 1 in 10 report meeting it in June, 1 in 24 in July, and 1 in 33 in August. Thus, according to the relative frequency of gales and fogs along the whole route in the month of June, it seems that the English vessel risks encountering five gales and no less than 22 fog banks, for June is the foggiest month in the year in the North At-

lantic. The American ship has the chance of meeting two gales, hut no fewer tliau 37 fog banks, as well as the chauces of ice, which is always met with in her route, hut much less frequently on the English side of the ocean. Calculating these dangers, therefore, by the tiinc which the whole expedition will heat sea, tiic chances will stand pretty nearly þÿ for the English ship three gales and 12 fog banks, for the American one gale and 23 fog hanks as well as ice. On the whole, therefore, the dangers may he fairly considered as nearly equal. Each country, then, shares equally in danger of completing this gigantic undertaking, þÿ to England belongs the glory of having conceived this glorious enterprise, having of advanced it with her wealth and science, and rendered it practicable through her manufacturing skill (BY Kt.ECTRlI TKI.RGRAPH.) A grave and more lasting cause of complaint than the stoppage of the Milan spring meeting is the heavy conscription. Making every allowance for the increase of population in the last 40 years, no conscription of Napoleon ever equalled this one, except perhaps that of 1814, when he was reduced to extremity by the losses ot the two previous years, and laid hands upon all the men he could find. It is the largest conscription ever known in Lombardy. It is certain, however, that in exchange for the recruits thus taken a number of soldiers

T - c R 0 I X A; V I Sr who have not served any very long time are allowed to return home on unlimited leave. The object of this exchange is doubtless to get all the yo(ig men of the country on the strength of the army. It may he styled, in some sort, an anti-revolutionary measure. The men released are liable to be called upon at any time to serve again. The exemptions from the conscription are few, except for physical defects. Only sons, and sons who are tho sole support of their families, arc the first to he spared ; after them come married men. The conscription is divided into five classes ; at 20 a young man is liable, and after 25 he is exempted. At 23, if he has not been taken, ho is allowed to marrv, hut tho priest is hound to warn him, in the presence of witnesses, that he is still liable to he summoned to the ranks. Novices and seminarists are also exempt, hut if they do not become monks or pciests they are subject to be called upon and taken as soldiers There are some smaller classes of the exempt, such as the first prize winners in painting and sculpture, but the whole put together constitute but a small minority of tho youth of the country. It is said to bo a not unfrequent practice with the authorities to pass over young men of the first class (2(1 y'ears of age) when they do not appear robust or fully developed, and to take them t%o following year, so that the service may have the advantage of 12 þÿmonths growth and increase of strdhgth. The complaints one hears of the severity of the

conscription are endless, and not the least is that of the high rate fixed by Government for the purchase of exemption, which constitutes an enormous tax upon families of moderate means who have several sons, and which sums of money, people here are well convinced, do not in the least diminish the amount.of compulsory servitude. If the Archduke Maximilian's attempts to win popularity have been very little rewarded at Milan, he does not seem to have been as yet more successful in conciliating public favour at Venice. A letter front the latter city, received The case is certainly a hard one. Permission i here yesterday, says that the attitude of the Venetians is anything but friendly, and that they have even made demonstrations which were hardly expected of them, since they are considered to he in general more indifferent about politics than the Milanese. On the 22d < list , the inuiversary of tlm insurrection of :S at Venice, tho hand was playing on the i ij/./.u li. .-an Marco, and the Archduke and Ar< hdticlicss ' ll their carriage and went to v tk among tin c.owd, whereupon the nuutej n proineuaders with one accord moved off , die adjoining Piazzctta and to the Iliva dci Sc.hiavoni, and continued their walk there, 1 ng the Prince and his suite in sole occupation of the great square. The hand, it is said had en expressly ordered to play on that day because the police bad heard that a gaont assemblage would take place in the piazza in like half a million of men under its colours. ! honour of (lie anniversary, and even that some

of the ladies proposed combining the national colours in tlioil costume. It was thought that that, by s' þÿm.o tint music it would appear as if . '. not the anniversary, was the cause of tlii assemblage. At the þÿArchduke receptions s scarcely any Italians appear þÿ much fewer even titan at Milau ; hut it must lie remembered tlmt scarcely any of the Venetian aristocracy are at present resident there. VVe hear also irom Venice of a disturbance that took place at the I enne, 1 beat re A daughter of Marsnal Nugent, married to an Italian nobleman, was in a oox with another lady and an Austrian ntlicer, and attracted some attention by her extravagant spirits and by' the loud tone -of her their schemes of social hostility to their mas- | conversation. Presently she look from the It certainly is a cat and dog life that | otiicer a cockade or plume (the exact nature of the object is not clearly stated) in which the Austrian colours, black and yellow, were combined, and placed it in her hair. The pit observed this and murmured loudly, and, as the lady persisted, the excitement and noise became such that her female companion left' the box iu alarm, and when she herself quitted the theatre, escorted by a number of officers, the crowd hissed and pressed upon them to such au extent that the police had to interfere. Such are the tales that reach us from Venice. 1 give them with great reserve, and without guaranteeing their correctness as regards details, for here it ik cxfjpemely difficult to sift
tho truth from the heap of exaggeration and misstatement, liut there is, no doubt, some fouudation fqr them ; qpd one thing certain is.

that the Venetians are not a bit better pleased to see the Austrian Viceroy among them than lie is to go there. Here, as, i suspect, iu most other parts of Italy, people seem well disposed to make a hero of Orsini. Ono does not, as at Turin, see his portrait and pamphlets concerning him figure In every shop window and on every bookstall, but other demonstrations have been made in lvs honour. At Padua, as you will perhaps already have heard, 800 students of that University' went to hear a mass, and, when this was over, they struck up the / Je profundis. It was well understood by everybody that this was for Orsini. 1 am told that this affair was immediately reported to Vienna, hut that the Government there decided that no notice should be taken of it. Amongst the students were several belonging to disiinguished Milanese families, which had sent them to Padua, iu pref (fence to Pavia, because the latter University has the reputation of being more exalte in its political views than the other. At Pavia au exactly similar demonstration was made. No particulars of it have reached me, except that it took place in the Church of Jesus. Here, at Milan, the fate of the Paris regicides has had the effect of eliciting a sign of life from the Democratic party, which, for the last two years, had disappeared from the scene. By some of its members a circular was sent out suggesting that mourning should be worn for Orsini The proposition found little favour with the great liberal and national party here ;

it was not intended to, and many of the eircu lars were sent to the police. The doctrine ot assassination forms no part of the political creed of the numerous and respectable national Italian party, and one hears the atrocious attempt in the Rue Lepelletier censured by these as severely as it could he by right-thinking men in any other country.

( from the Condon Times, April I/., HOUSE OF COMMONS, Friday, April hi THE CASE OF THE CAGLIARI. Mr. HKADLAM asked the Chancellor ot the, Exchequer whether lie had as yet received the opinions of the law. officers of the Crown on the subject of the Cagliari ; and, if so, whether he could state, to the House what course the Government intended to take? The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER þÿ In the, matter of the Cagliari there are two One, is what I may call the national question questions involved, which are really distinct. . the other the international question. The first concerns the treatment of our two eouutryineri. Park and Watt. With respect to that part of the question we have received the opinions of the Crown officers, and their opinions on that subject are, unanimous. They are of opinion that the detention and imprisonment of Park and Watt were illegal. (Hear, hear ) In consequence of having received that opinion.

we have, after all that deliberation which so serious a matter demanded, addressed a despatch to the Minister of the King of Naples ; and the Secretary of State has demanded compensation for the our grievances which have been Park and Watt. (Loud experienced by cries two of " Hear !") With res- countrymen, pect to the international question, that, as the lion, and learned gentleman well understands, is a question quite distinct and separate from the other, in which England is only interested as all other maritime nations are. On that wo have not yet received the opinions ot the Crown officers. T may, in explanation of what may appear an unaccountable delay, state that, , although on Saturday last very important documents were received and submitted to the Attorney -General and his colleagues, yet his time has been so absorbed during the last few days in the hiin possible for State trials that it has not been yet to give those documents all the consideration they require. (Hear, hear.)

FRANCE. (from ol'r own correspondent. PARIS, Tuesday, April 10, 6 p.m Whether any particular information has been received from London to-day in official quarters 1 cannot say, but it is affirmed that a good deal of uneasiness prevails then respecting the present position of the English Cabinet. Its friends here seem to have serious doubts, or rather they all but despair, of Lord Derby being able to maintain himself long in power. The debates in Parliament, particularly with reference to the defences of the English coast, have suggested matter for reflection. The faults which have been committed since the 14th of January cannot, it is true, be undone, but they are said to he deeply and, 1 believe, seriously regretted. Hopes are expressed that Lord Cowley's presence in London before the arrival of Marshal l'elissier will aid in removing any difficulty as yet in the way. 1 am assured on good authority that within the last live or six days the Emperor declared to a person with whom he was conversing that his determination was not only to have no quarrel with England, but to remain her friend and ally. If this be sincere, as I trust it is, the Emperor will show his accustomed sagacity in abiding bv that line of policy.

The Debuts, of Monday, has a leader on the subject of our occupation of the Isle of Periin. It says that, although it was premature in stating that a collective note had been addressed to England by the Cabinets of France and Russia, yet " it is true, and should surprise no one, that this affair of Periin has recently been I he subject of a serious conversation between Count Walewski and Count Kisseleff, Ambassador of Russia." It then gives its own version of the several occupations, combats the deductions of Mr. Vernon Smith, and concludes : þÿ " Under any circumstances, Turkey protests against this new occupation, which is effected without her authorisation and under totally different circumstances from those in which the two countries found themselves in 1790. She vindicates firmly her rights over the Isle of Perim, which she will neither gratuitously cede nor sell to England. The Sultan refuses to grant the tirinan asked from him to authorise the piercing of the Isthmus of Suez, at least until the English restore Perim. The Porto knows the value which the whole of Europe, except the English Government, attach it to the execution of this grand project. Is not, then, as if Turkey appealed to Europe, to all the co signatory Powers of the Treaty of Paris, against this open violation of her territory, against this attack made against the independence and integrity of the Ottoman Empire 1" In another part it declares l'crini to be a second Gibraltar." As this spot is now the subject of

a political " difficulty," the subjoined information lruy prove interesting When the 1' rench took possession of Egypt in 1799, the English began to fortify the island, but quitted it soon after 1801, in which year Egypt was restored to the Turks. Somewhat to the south of Perim, and close to the African coast, is an island which is well known as the " Aclit Bruder" (it is marked in English charts as "High Bro thers"), and of this British troops are said recently to have taken possession. When the English returned to Perim about a year ago they found that no one had meddled with the

The Sardinian Government, in a circular issued upon the subject of the Cagliari, says that the explanations hitherto exchanged between the two Cabinets of Turin and Naples having led to no result, a grave conflict is im- a minent, for the Government of Sardinia has right to reparation, aud is resolved on obtaining, by reprisals or iu any other way, a satisfaction for its insulted flag, and complete justice for its subjects violently despoiled. A profound sensation lias been created by the publication in the Piedmontese official Gazette of two documents purporting to he a second letter from Orsini to lite Emperor Napoleon, and Orsini's will. There seems to he no room to doubt tliat they are genuine; and it is generally 1>elieved that Napoleon lias himself instigated the publication, though why they should not have appeared in Paris is somewhat of a mystery. The French are loud in extolling the changed views at Orsini. The letter is as follows : þÿ " To his Majesty Napoleon III., Emperor of the French. In a

EXTRAORDINARY ACT OF BRIGAN- DAGE NEAR ROME. A letter from Rome in the Univtrs contains the following extraordinary tale: þÿ In the cathedral of Velletri, near Rome, was an image of the Virgin, nearly covered with gold, and decked out with necklaces, rings, and jewellery, and it was held in great veneration by the people. In the Holy Week it was, according to custom, screened from view by a curtain, and on Holy Thursday some person contrived to steal it. On Good Friday the archpriest of the cathedral received a note thus conceived: þÿ "I, the undersigned, know the thief, and the spot in which is deposited the image of the Madonna, and I will make revela tions on three conditions þÿ impunity lor myself, the release of my brother, who is condemned to death, and a pension of ten crowns a month. þÿ Vendetta."The archpriest having ascertained that the image really had been abstracted, communicated the strange epistle to the delegate, Mgr Giordani. Instead of seeking at once for the writer of the letter, this dignitary applied to Rome for orders, and and the. the effect that would he produced, amongst Pope, fearing the total loss of the image, the people, directed that the first condition of the bandit should he accepted, but, that the other two should he rejected. Vendetta having learned this resolution, spread amongst the p (topic of Velletri the news of the robbery of the image, which the clergy of the cathedral had kept secret, and he wrote to the clergy that he would be content with impunity for himself and with 500 crowns paid down. On

Saturday the people went en masse to the church, and waited with anxiety for the arrival of that part of the service in which the crucifixes and images are uncovered ; hut the veil which had covered the image of the Madonna was not removed. On Sunday the people again went to the church, but as the image was not displayed, they became excited, and murmured ; and at length some of them got on the altar and tore down the curtain. The rumour was then spread by friends of Vendetta that it was the Jesuits who had stolen the Madonna; and the excited people believing the falsehood, broke into the convent occupied by the Jesuits, which is adjacent to the cathedral, and with cries of "La Madonna nostra!" completely sacked it, and ill-treated the reverend fathers. Shortly after the suffragan bishop ascended the pulpit, and exhorted the people who remained in the church to be calm, hut they would not listen to him. There is no garrison except 10 or 12 veterans in the town, so that no opposition could be made to the mob. AVhen the bishop descended from the pulpit a scarcely credible scene occurred ; the hrigaud Vendetta, armed sed the people þÿ with a poignard, ascended it, and thus addres- " Be patient ! The good fathers are innocent! It is 1 who stole the Madonna ! But I will only restore it when the Government, to whom I grant a delay till Monday evening, shall have consented to the compact I have proposed to it. Be calm, therefore, and shout no more ! 1 warn you, in conclusion, that my companions are armed as well

as I !" What followed that harangue we have not yet heard ; hut a deputation of the municipality and chapter of Velletri have arrived here, and have had an interview with the l'ope. Orders have been issued' to dispatch a troop of gendarmes on to Swiss infantry horseback and a company of Velletri to establish order. From other sources we learn that Vendetta has been transferred to prison in Rome, where he will probably meet with no great indulgence; 50 or GO of the most active rioters have been arrested at Velletri, and that town will continue to he occupied by the military until judicial proceedings are complete''.

All this was to our satisfaction ; but at that moment a flash of lightning illumined the whole arch of the heavens, lighting the prairie as with a thousand torches. It was none of the pale lavendercoloured light, seen in northern climes, but a brilliant blaze, that appeared to pervade all space, and almost rivalled the brightness of day. In the former, the flashes are quick and shortlived, and the intervals of darkness also of short duration. Rolts pierce the clouds in straight, lance-like shafts, or forking and zigzag, followed by thunder in loud uucqual hursts, and dashes of intermittent rain. The other is very distinct from this; there arc no shafts or bolts, but a steady blaze which fills the whole firmament with a white quivering light, lasting many seconds of time, and followed by long intervals of amorphous darkness. Rube watched the guerrilleros, permitting his head to be seen by them. My eyes were bent upou the rocky wall, but through the thick darkness I looked in vain for our comrade. 1 listened to hear how he was progressing : I could distinguish a slight scratching against the cliff, each moment higher aud farther away ; hut Garey climbed with a moceasiued foot, and the noise was too faint to reach the ears of our enemies. O for a long interval of darkness ! It appeard a long one ; perhaps it was not five minutes, but it felt twice that, before the lightning again blazed forth. With the flash, I ran my eyes up the precipitous wall. OGod! Garey was still upon its face, scarcely midway up. He was standing on a ledge þÿ his body flattened against the rock þÿ and with his arms extended horizontally, lie presented the appearance of a man crucified upou the cliff ! So long as the glare lasted, he remained it! this attitude, motionless as the rock itself. 1 turned with anxious look towards the guerrilleros. I heard no voice ; 1 observed no movement. Thank Heaven ! they saw him not ! Near where ho was resting, some bushes of the trailing cedar grew out of the clifl'; their dark foliage mottled its white lace, rendering the form of the climber less conspicuous Another long spell of darkness, another blaze of light. I scanned the gorge : no human form was visi-

ble. I saw a dark lino that, like a crack, vertically intersected the cliff from parapet to base : it was the rope Garey had carried up. He had reached the summit in saf ety ! It was my turn next þÿ for Rube insisted on retaining the post of danger þÿ and with my rifle slung ou my back, I stood ready. I had given the parting whisper to my brave steed, and pressed his velvet muzzle to my cheek. Willi the last flicker of the electric gleam, I seized the hanging lazo, and drew myself upward. 1 had confidence in the rope : I knew it was fastened above, or safe in the strong grasp of Garey. With its aid, the ascent was rendered easy. I experienced no difficulty in climbing from ledge to ledge, and before the light came again, I had reached the crest of the clifl. We lay flat among the hushes that grew by the very brink, scarcely shewing our faces to the front. I saw that the rope had been fastened round the trunk of a small tree. Presently we perceived by its jerking that Rube had begun his ascent. Shortly alter, we could hear him sprawling and scratching upward, and then his thin dark form loomed over the edge of the cliff, and dead beat for breath, he staggered silently into the bushes beside us. Even in the darkuess, I noticed something peculiar in his appearance : his head looked smaller, hut Iliad no time to question him. We waited only for another glance at the guerrilleros ; they were still at their posts, evidently unconscious of our movcmcuts. Rube's catskin cap, cunningly adjusted upon the boulder,

satisfied theni that we were still at ouis; and explained, moreover, the oddness I had observed about the upper story of the trapper. Rube had now recovered wind ; aud gathering up the rope, we stole away over the fablesummit to search for a place of desct nt Ou reaching the opposite side, we at once found what we wanted þÿ a tree near the edge of the cliff. Many small pines grew upon the escarpment ; and selecting one, we knotted the ropo securely around its trunk There was yet much to be done before any of us could attempt the descent. We knew that the cliff was more than a hundred feet in vertical height, and to glide down a rope of that length is a trying feat, worthy the most expert of tars. None of us might bo able to accomplish it; the first could be lowered down easily enough, and this was our intention ; so might the second ; hut the other would have to glide down the rope. We were not long delayed by the contemplation of this obstacle : my comrades were men of quick thought ; and a plan to lesson the difficulty soon suggested itself. Their knives were out in a trice : a sapling was procured, and cut into intervals along the rope. Our ' -Jacob's ladder' short pieces ; these were notched, and tied at was ready.

It still remained to make sure that the rope was of sufficient length. The knots had somewhat shortened it ; but this point was soon settled with like ingenuity. A small stone was tied listened : we hoard the dull ' thump' ol the stone to one end, aud then dropped over the clifl'. We upon the prairie turf. The rope therefore reached to the ground. It was again drawn up, the stone taken out, and the noose fastened around the body of Rube, under bis armpits. He was the lightest, and for this reason had been chosen to make the tirst descent, as he would least try the strength of the rope þÿ still a doubtful point. The ascent had not proved it þÿ for in climbing up, but onehalf of our weight had been upon it, our feet resting either against the clifl', or upon its ledges. On reaching the plain, Rube was to submit the rope to trial, before either Garey or I should attempt to go down This lie was to do by adding a largo stone to his own weight þÿ making both at least equal to that of Garey, who was by far the heaviest of the party. All being arranged, the old trapper slid silently over the edge of the cliff þÿ Garey and I giving out the rope slowly, and with caution. Foot by foot, and yard by yard, it was drawn through our hands by the weight of' the descending body, now lost to our sight over the brow of the eliff. Still slowly, and with caution, we allowed the lazo to pass, taking care that it should glide gradually, so as not to jerk, and cause the body of our comrade to vibrate with too much violence

against the rocks. We were both seated close together, our faces turned to the plain. More than three-quarters of the rope had passed from us, and we were congratulating ourselves that the trial would soon be over, when, to our dismay, the strain ceased with a suddenness that caused both of us we heard the ' twang' of the snapping rope, fol- to recoil upon our backs ! At the same instant, lowed by a sharp cry from below ! We sprang to our feet, and mechauically recommenced hauling upon the rope. The weight was uo longer upon it ; it was light packthread, and retained to our hands without effort. Desisting, we fronted to each other, but not for an explanation Neither required it; neither uttered a word. The ease was clear : the rope had broken ; our comrade had been hurled to the earth ' With a simultaneous impulse, we dropped upon our knees; and, crawling forward to the brink of the precipice, looked over and downward Wu could see nothing in the dark abysm that frown d below ; and we waited till the light should break forth again. groan wo heard We listened with ears keenly set. Was it a - a cry of agony .' No ; its repetition told us what it was þÿ the howl of the prairie-wolf No human voice reached our ears. Alas, no! Even a cry of pain would have been welcome, since it would have told us our cotnradistill lived But no, he was silent þÿ dead þÿ per haps broken to atoms ! It was long ere the lightning gleamed again Before it did, we heard voices. They came from the bottom of the cliff directly under us; hut

there were two, and neither was the voice of tin trapper. It is easy to distinguish the full intonation of the Saxon from the shrill treble of the sons of Anahuae. The voices were those of our foes. Presently the light discovered them to us. Two there were. They were on horseback, moving on the plain below, and close in to the cliff. We saw thein distinctly, hut we saw not what we had expected þÿ the mangled body of our comrade ! The gleam, long continued, had given us full time to scrutinise the ground. We could have distinguished upon it any object as large as a cat. Rube, living or dead, was certainly not there ! Hud lie fallen into the hands of the guerrilla: The two we saw carried lances, but no prisoner. It was not likely they had captured him ; besides, we knew that llube, unless badly crippled, would never have surrendered without a struggle, and neither shot nor shout had been heard. Wo were soon relieved from all uneasiness on this score. The brigands continued their conversation, and the light breeze wafted their voices upwards, so that we could distinguish part ot what was said. To be continued
